claims.text: Wear resistance initially improves as ambient temperature rises from room temperature to approximately 800°C because a stable tribo-oxide film forms.
Wear resistance degrades rapidly above approximately 800°C.
High-temperature degradation is caused in part by FCC-to-HCP transformation.
High-temperature degradation is caused in part by sigma-phase precipitation.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between an HEA coating and its transition-metal matrix can induce cracking.
The starting coating has a metastable FCC or BCC solid-solution structure.
The coating contains oxidation-associated elements such as Al and Cr and phase-transforming elements such as Co, Fe, Mn, and Ni.
The coating will be tested by reciprocating sliding in air while ambient temperature is increased from room temperature to 900°C.
At 800–900°C, tribo-oxidation can generate a continuous protective oxide film that shields the metal from direct mechanical contact and reduces wear depth.
High local Cr concentration can promote sigma-phase formation at grain boundaries in an HEA.
Increasing temperature under the proposed ambient-pressure wear conditions can trigger an FCC-to-HCP transformation within the coating.
Brittle phase formation reduces coating ductility and fracture toughness.
Mismatch-induced microcracking compromises the protective layer and accelerates wear.
The wear-depth curve is non-monotonic, decreasing up to approximately 800°C and then increasing sharply above 800°C.
At room temperature, wear is dominated by abrasion and no stable protective oxide film persists.
For AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5, the degradation boundary occurs above approximately 800°C.
The critical degradation temperature depends on alloy composition, including Cr content, and on coating–matrix thermal-expansion mismatch.
The cited FCC/HCP phase boundary is pressure-dependent, so a temperature-only wear boundary is an extrapolation from high-pressure evidence.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis, outcome, and boundary predict rapid degradation above about 800°C, whereas the mechanism states that a continuous protective film reduces wear at 800–900°C. The cited same-alloy evidence also reports protection at both 800°C and 900°C.

FCC-to-HCP transformation is presented as a high-temperature degradation mechanism, but the uncertainty field acknowledges that the cited phase-transition evidence is pressure-dependent; that evidence specifically reports the inverse HCP-to-FCC transition upon heating.
